name: Diego Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What is a normal day on site?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the carpentry from floor joists to roof on small house builds. I earned a trade certificate and know how a wrong line on a slab follows you all the way upstairs. I like seeing a family walk through a frame I set straight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what happens outside the weekday job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I build decks on weekends and use AI every day for garden designs and material lists. My wife Marisol works part-time at a pharmacy; we have two children in school, a mortgage and less than a month saved. The main builder pays low, and there are few similar jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the house crew my design app is still useful even if the grand promises fade. It helps customers see a deck before I buy timber, but a picture does not set a post straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage as lead carpenter is low, and the deck work on weekends has not made a proper reserve yet. Marisol and I have a mortgage and two children in school; a slow month leaves less than four weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep framing houses on weekdays and using my existing AI design and pricing tools for weekend deck quotes. If two extra paid deck orders come in this spring, I would send the profit after materials straight to the trailer loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our thin cash, even in a quiet future. I like the tool, but customers still have to sign and pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does a deck order leave after materials?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It varies with timber and travel, which is why I count profit only after the customer pays. A customer sketch does not pay the trailer loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you add a new AI tool now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The daily design and materials apps are enough, and I still measure the garden before ordering a board.

say: I would call my existing **AI design app** useful for showing decks to customers.
I would remind the crew that **site measurements** still decide whether a frame fits.
think: My **low wage** and less than one month saved keep the household tight.
Weekend **deck profit** is uneven until customers pay and materials are covered.
do: Keep **weekday house framing** and existing deck quotes.
Pay extra **trailer loan principal** only from two additional paid deck profits after materials.
feel: **Anxious** about current cash despite enjoying a useful AI tool.
S0.quote: A customer sketch does not pay the trailer loan.
fieldNote: His own side business is **existing work**, so continuing quotes is not a new side-income action.
The extra debt payment depends on **paid orders** and net profit, not optimistic enquiries.

steps.text: Keep weekday framing and existing AI deck quotes
Pay extra trailer loan principal only from two paid deck profits after materials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI buying could save the builder time, but a delivered window still needs someone to see whether the opening is square. I would ask management for a real-site trial before changing our quotas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office might shrink and the contractor could expect more frames per day. My own framing hours could get cut between jobs, and fewer local builders means the deck business would have to carry more of our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI ordering screen if the company gives me access, then compare its first two timber lists with the actual slabs. I would also stop taking unpaid site errands for the manager, so paid deck hours are not squeezed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, but I have a second way to earn if customers keep booking. A lovely screen is not a signed deck job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you protect the weekend work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need Friday evening to measure gardens and send firm quotes. If the builder needs an extra errand, it should be on paid company time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy another trailer now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The first one still has a loan. I would wait until completed paid decks, not enquiries, cover a purchase.

say: I would ask for a **real-site trial** before AI buying changes framing quotas.
I would tell management that **delivered windows** still need a carpenter checking the opening.
think: My **framing hours** could shrink while nearby replacement jobs remain scarce.
The **deck business** helps only when customers sign, pay and leave a margin.
do: Learn the new **AI ordering screen** with company access and compare two timber lists.
Protect **paid deck quoting time** by declining unpaid site errands.
feel: **Anxious** about possible job hours, with uncertain paid side orders as a partial fallback.
S1.quote: A lovely screen is not a signed deck job.
fieldNote: He is eager to learn a **new ordering control**, beyond existing design apps.
The side business is already running; he refuses to count **enquiries as income**.

steps.text: Learn AI ordering controls with company access and check two real timber lists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that thinking AI in 2028 can price a house, but it cannot lift roof trusses. Around 2031 robots may do that too, and I would want the first trial on a real muddy plot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the builder to cut framing crews once capable robots arrive, and I could lose a large part of my weekday wage. The deck orders may not replace it, while Marisol’s part-time pharmacy wage and our tiny reserve cannot carry the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid framing shifts and ask the builder for a posted paid robot-site supervisor role before buying any course. If such a vacancy appears with funded training and a mortgage-covering wage, I would complete the course and apply; if no offer comes, I would seek posted carpentry work farther out only for enough net pay after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would lie awake counting how long we could keep the mortgage current. I cannot build an extra weekday wage out of thin air.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop the deck business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would keep paid orders, but I would not promise they fill the whole wage gap. Marisol and I need the main mortgage payment covered first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far would you search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Far enough to reach an advertised carpenter job, even if the drive is long. I would take it only after a firm offer covers fuel, travel time and the mortgage.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** handles pricing before 2031 robots can frame muddy sites.
I would demand a **real-plot trial** before the builder cuts carpenters.
think: I expect a major **weekday wage cut** and may lose my framing post.
Deck orders and Marisol’s **part-time pay** may not cover the mortgage.
do: Keep **paid framing shifts** while the builder offers them.
Complete **funded robot supervision training** only for a posted paid mortgage-covering role.
Seek **advertised distant carpentry work** only for a firm net-pay offer covering travel and mortgage.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected large income loss with less than a month saved.
S2.quote: I cannot build an extra weekday wage out of thin air.
fieldNote: His anxiety becomes alarm because he expects a **major wage loss** and has almost no reserve.
Both the new role and distant job require **posted paid offers** that cover mortgage and travel.

steps.text: Keep paid weekday framing shifts while builder work exists
Complete funded robot supervisor course only for a posted mortgage-covering paid role
Seek posted distant carpentry work only with firm net pay covering travel and mortgage
Apply for posted supervisor role after funded training only at mortgage-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets us test a framing robot on uneven ground before it gets a whole housing plot. I would volunteer to record where it fails, if the builder pays for those trial hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 may change pricing and orders first. Robots arrive around 2034, when my children will still have school costs and my mortgage will still be there; the extra years help me build savings from the deck work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep both paid jobs this year and move an extra set amount from each completed deck profit into our emergency account after materials and the trailer payment. If the builder posts a paid robot-site lead vacancy with funded controls training, I would apply and take the training on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about 2034, but less cornered than in the fast case. I can learn the controls if the work behind them is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What amount can you save from a finished deck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twenty from a paid job after materials, tax and the trailer loan payment, if a margin remains. I would not take an emergency deposit from the household grocery money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you log in a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot losing a stud line when the slab is out of square. I would write down the measurement and stop the next lift until a person checks it.

say: I would require **uneven-ground trials** before 2034 framing robots take whole plots.
I would volunteer for **paid trial hours** to log errors if the builder offers them.
think: My **mortgage and school costs** continue through the robot date.
Five years could let paid **deck profits** build a small emergency reserve.
do: Save **twenty per deck** after materials, tax and trailer payments if a margin remains.
Apply for a **paid lead role** only with funded controls training on paid time.
feel: **Anxious** about future weekday pay, with more time to prepare from actual profit.
S3.quote: I would not take an emergency deposit from the household grocery money.
fieldNote: The new saving comes from **completed net deck profits**, not a transfer of existing cash.
He conditions training and applications on a **posted paid role** with funded paid time.

steps.text: Save twenty per paid deck only after materials tax and trailer payments leave profit
Apply for posted paid robot-site lead work only with funded controls training on paid time
Learn robot controls on paid time only for a posted funded lead role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell young builders ten years is enough to master framing before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. Apprentices should learn to read a crooked slab with their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty six at the robot date, still needing a wage unless the deck business has grown into steady paid work. We have less than a month saved today, so the long runway is useful but not a cushion by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep house framing and paid deck orders during 2026. I would set aside ten from each paid deck profit after materials and debt, and in the first year after 2036 I would compare actual framing hours with posted vacancies before choosing any new course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our present cash, but the decade gives us time to build something real. I would rather teach my children careful work than promise them a perfect machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the builder for your own business now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would need several months of booked and paid decks at a margin that covers the mortgage before giving up the weekday wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A frame on a slab that looks level at one corner and drops at the other. A drawing is a start, but the tape and your eyes decide the cut.

say: I would protect **framing apprenticeship** before 2036 thinking AI and 2039 robots arrive.
I would teach apprentices to measure **crooked slabs** rather than trust a clean drawing.
think: I will still need **paid work** in 2039 unless the deck business earns steadily.
The **thin reserve** today keeps the family anxious despite the longer runway.
do: Keep **2026 framing** and paid deck orders while they bring income.
Save **deck profit** only after materials and debt leave a margin.
feel: **Anxious** about current cash, with time to grow real profits.
S4.quote: A drawing is a start, but the tape and your eyes decide the cut.
fieldNote: He does not treat a future business exit as certain; it needs **months of paid margins**.
The new savings step draws on **net deck profit** rather than existing household money.

steps.text: Keep weekday framing and paid deck orders during 2026
Save ten per paid deck only after materials and trailer debt leave profit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could take a big part of my weekday framing wage by 2031. A posted paid supervisor role with funded controls training, or a firm carpenter offer covering travel and mortgage, would help us act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a customer has paid before counting the deck as an income plan. A drawing on my phone cannot buy the children dinner.

headlineQuote: A drawing on my phone cannot buy the children dinner.
portrait: **Diego**, 43, leads house framing with a trade certificate, low wages and less than one month of expenses saved.
His weekend **deck business** uses AI daily, but paid orders are uneven and Marisol’s pharmacy wage is part-time.
A mortgage, two school-age children and **few nearby jobs** make a large loss of weekday pay serious.
The **2028 case** alarms him; he seeks funded paid controls work or a firm distant offer covering travel and housing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a major part of his weekday framing wage by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A posted **paid supervisor role** with funded training or a firm mortgage-covering carpenter offer would help.
